![](BlogPost03Cover.png){width="500px"}
In 2000, Americans aged 65 and older who worked during the survey reference 
week averaged about 30 hours of work. Those aged 16–24 averaged roughly 33. By 
2024, their positions had reversed: older workers averaged about 33 hours, 
younger workers about 31. Older workers had not become the longest-working 
group, but this reversal complicates a familiar question: Are Americans working
more or less? The answer depends on whose working week we examine.

That distinction matters because employment counts measure how many people work,
not how much time they contribute. Someone working twenty hours and someone 
working forty can each count as one employed person, despite different labor 
inputs and time available for education, caregiving, or other activities. 
Comparing age groups can reveal changes hidden within national averages. 
Separating main-job hours from other-job hours adds another question: 
**How did actual weekly working hours change across age groups between 2000 and 2024, and where did those changes occur?**

![](figures/fig1_total_hours_by_age.png){width="95%"}

Workers aged 25–64 occupy a relatively stable corridor in Figure 1, generally 
averaging around 39–42 hours. The youngest and oldest groups sit below that 
corridor, but move in different directions. Younger workers’ hours fell early 
in the period, declined further around 2009, and subsequently recovered 
somewhat. Older workers’ hours generally increased, reaching a higher level 
around 2021 before retreating. The middle groups also ended below their 
starting levels, although their declines were interrupted by recoveries. This 
is a story of divergence and fluctuation, rather than a uniform shortening of 
the working week.

The analysis uses **IPUMS CPS** Basic Monthly microdata covering 300 months from 
January 2000 through December 2024. It retains civilian workers aged 16 and 
older who actually worked during the reference week, had positive sampling 
weights, and had valid information for all three hours measures. Monthly 
averages use the individual weight **WTFINL**; annual estimates average the twelve 
monthly estimates equally. These are actual hours worked last week, rather than 
usual or contracted hours. Consequently, the older group’s increase describes 
people who were working; it does not establish that older Americans generally 
worked more or became more likely to hold jobs.

![](figures/fig2_main_job_hours_by_age.png){width="95%"}

Separating the working week reveals where most of the movement occurred. 
Figure 2 closely resembles Figure 1: older workers’ main-job hours increased, 
younger workers’ hours declined, and the middle groups retained their 
fluctuations. Because the figures share a vertical scale, their levels and 
movements are directly comparable. The age divergence therefore appears 
primarily in the main job, directing attention toward changes in principal 
work arrangements.

![](figures/fig3_other_job_hours_by_age.png){width="95%"}

Other jobs operate on a much smaller scale. In 2024, their contribution 
averaged approximately 0.6–0.85 hours per week across age groups, with workers 
aged 45–54 highest. But “less than an hour” does not describe a typical 
multiple-job holder’s additional workload. Confirmed single-job holders 
contribute zeros, spreading additional hours across the entire retained sample. 
This average reflects both how common multiple jobs are and how many additional 
hours their holders work.

![](figures/fig4_main_job_share_by_age.png){width="95%"}
![](figures/fig5_other_job_share_by_age.png){width="95%"}


The shares reinforce this interpretation: main jobs consistently account for 
approximately 98% of total hours. Figure 4’s narrow vertical range makes small 
changes look pronounced. Meanwhile, younger workers often have relatively high 
other-job shares without the highest other-job hours, partly because their total
hours are lower. These annual shares divide average component hours by average 
total hours; they are not averages of individual shares. Retained 
inconsistencies between reported components and totals mean the two shares need 
not sum exactly to 100%.

The reversal remains descriptive. Older workers’ average could rise because 
individuals work longer, because shorter-hours workers leave employment, or 
through both processes. These repeated age-group comparisons do not follow the 
same individuals over time. Actual reference-week hours can also reflect 
temporary absences, while annual averaging conceals within-year changes. 
Complete-case selection, retained top-coded values, and inconsistent records 
may affect estimates. Without survey-design confidence intervals or 
significance tests, visible differences cannot establish statistical 
significance or causation.

**The central finding is a reversal between the youngest and oldest working groups, concentrated in main-job hours.** Explaining it requires learning who stayed in work, who left, and how their principal jobs changed.
